 6 weather alerts in effect Arizona drivers warned after Toyota, Volkswagen recalls over stall, fire risks 
 To walk through what to do if your car is affected, On Your Side spoke with Valley attorney Sargon Khananisho, founder of Sargon Law Group. By Christine Stanwood Published : Oct. 20, 2026 at 5:42 PM MST | Updated : 9 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google PHOENIX (AZFamily) — It seems like new car recalls are reported all the time, and it can be easy to tune them out. But Valley drivers may want to tune in for a tune-up sooner than later.
 Two major recalls right now affect thousands of Arizonans:
 Toyota is recalling about 30,000 2026 RAV4 Plug-in Hybrids that can suddenly lose power and shut down at high speeds. 
 Volkswagen is recalling more than 22,500 ID.4 EVs over a high-voltage battery fire risk. 
 Valley attorney: Don’t wait for a crash you can prevent
 To walk through what to do if your car is affected, On Your Side spoke with Valley attorney Sargon Khananisho, founder of Sargon Law Group, about cases he deals with on a regular basis.
 “That can be a major hazard for you and your family,” Khananisho said of a high-speed loss of power.
 Now in his 15th year as an attorney, Khananisho said his team focuses first on what happened in a crash.
 “We look and get an expert to investigate whether that loss of power was a contributing factor to the accident, or was it a third party operating error.”
 He said they can make a claim to the manufacturer to see if a defect was a factor that led to injuries.
 “There’s constant production of vehicles on a regular basis, all different types. And understanding that there are recalls. And to be aware of those recalls before something arises that can cause a crash,” Khananisho said.
 Why getting the fix helps you long-term
 Khananisho said servicing your recalled vehicle helps in two ways:
 1. It preserves the longevity of your vehicle. “Usually you want to keep your car as long as you possibly can before you have to go into a new one,” he said. 
 2. Safety. Call the dealership ahead of time with your VIN, let them know you looked it up and there’s a recall. They will coordinate a drop-off timeframe, and usually they will put you in a rental vehicle because “it’s not something of your own doing,” Khananisho said. 
 Is it your responsibility to look for recalls?
 Dealerships and manufacturers do provide notices, Khananisho said.
 “I’ve been in this industry long enough to know that some things don’t always come to light, and sometimes you need to go searching for that information to make sure you’re protected for the best for you and your family,” he said. 
 How to check if your car is recalled in 2 minutes
 Find your car’s VIN on your windshield on the driver’s side or on the inside of the driver’s door. 
 Go to nhtsa.gov/recalls and enter the 17-digit VIN. 
 Call your dealer if there’s an open recall to schedule the free fix. 
 Khananisho suggests checking quarterly. Not every recall will lead to a malfunction that could cause a crash, he said, but hearing about recalls every day is not something to be fearful of — it’s something to act on.
